For a finite reversible chain $(X,P,\pi)$, let $H_0=\{f:\sum_x\pi_xf_x=0\}$ with the weighted inner product from [[lem-qa-17-reversible-transition-self-adjoint-on-l2-pi]]. Define its **absolute spectral gap** by

$$\delta_{\mathrm{abs}}(P):=1-\|P|_{H_0}\|_{2,\pi}.$$

The norm of the restriction to the zero subspace is $0$ by [[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]], so a one-state chain has absolute gap $1$. No irreducibility or aperiodicity is built into this definition: a reducible chain with a nonconstant stationary vector in $H_0$ can have gap $0$, and a periodic chain can have gap $0$ because of an eigenvalue $-1$. The eigenvalue form of the definition is proved in [[thm-qa-17-absolute-gap-eigenvalue-characterization]].

For a finite reversible chain $(X,P,\pi)$, equip $\mathbb C^X$ with $\langle f,g\rangle_\pi:=\sum_x\pi_x f_x\overline{g_x}$. Then $P$ is self-adjoint for this inner product, and the mean-zero subspace

$$H_0:=\{f:\sum_x\pi_xf_x=0\}=\{f:\langle f,\mathbf 1\rangle_\pi=0\}$$

is invariant under $P$. The restriction $P|_{H_0}$ is therefore a well-defined endomorphism and is self-adjoint for the restricted inner product.

Let $(X,P,\pi)$ be a finite reversible chain and let $f:X\to\mathbb C$. Define $\|f\|_{2,\pi}^2:=\sum_x\pi_x|f_x|^2$ and $(Pf)_x:=\sum_yP_{xy}f_y$. Then

$$\|Pf\|_{2,\pi}^2\le\|f\|_{2,\pi}^2,$$

so $P$ is a contraction on the finite weighted inner-product space $L^2(X,\pi)$. Detailed balance is not needed for this inequality beyond the stated stationary-law hypotheses.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let $T:V\to V$
be linear. Then $T$ is normal if and only if $V$ has an orthonormal basis
consisting of eigenvectors of $T$.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ and let $T:V\to V$ be linear. A scalar $\lambda\in F$ is an **eigenvalue** of $T$ when there is a nonzero vector $v\in V$ such that

$$T(v)=\lambda v.$$

Such a vector is an **eigenvector belonging to $\lambda$**. The **eigenspace** belonging to $\lambda$ is

$$E_\lambda(T):=\ker(T-\lambda I_V)=\{v\in V:T(v)=\lambda v\}.$$

Thus $E_\lambda(T)$ is a linear subspace and always contains $0_V$, while $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue exactly when $E_\lambda(T)\ne\{0_V\}$. The **spectrum of $T$ over $F$** is

$$\sigma_F(T):=\{\lambda\in F:\lambda\text{ is an eigenvalue of }T\}.$$

In particular, the unique endomorphism of the zero space has empty spectrum.

derivations.claim: If $H_0=\{0\}$, the restriction has zero domain, so its operator norm is $0$ by [F1] and the gap is $1$. Otherwise, [F2] and [F4] give an orthonormal eigenbasis $e_1,\ldots,e_m$ of $H_0$. Each eigenvalue is real: if $Pe_j=\lambda_je_j$, self-adjointness and [F7] give $\lambda_j\|e_j\|^2=\langle Pe_j,e_j\rangle_\pi=\langle e_j,Pe_j\rangle_\pi=\overline{\lambda_j}\|e_j\|^2$. [F5] identifies these eigenvalues as the spectrum of the restriction.

Write $f=\sum_j c_je_j$. Orthonormality gives $\|f\|_{2,\pi}^2=\sum_j|c_j|^2$ and $\|Pf\|_{2,\pi}^2=\sum_j|\lambda_j|^2|c_j|^2\le (\max_j|\lambda_j|)^2\|f\|_{2,\pi}^2$, with equality at an eigenvector whose eigenvalue has largest modulus. Therefore $\|P|_{H_0}\|_{2,\pi}=\max_j|\lambda_j|$.
By [F3] the restriction norm is at most $1$, and it is nonnegative by definition; substituting step 1.2 into [F1] proves both the eigenvalue formula and $0\le\delta_{\mathrm{abs}}(P)\le1$.

If $Pf=f$ and $f\notin\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf1\}$, put $c=\sum_x\pi_xf_x$ and $h=f-c\mathbf1$. The normalization $\sum_x\pi_x=1$ gives $h\in H_0$, while $h\ne0$ because $f$ is not constant. Since $P\mathbf1=\mathbf1$, $Ph=Pf-cP\mathbf1=h$. Thus $1$ is an eigenvalue of $P|_{H_0}$ and step 1.2 gives $\|P|_{H_0}\|=1$, so [F1] gives $\delta_{\mathrm{abs}}(P)=0$.

For a finite row-stochastic kernel $(X,P)$, let $\mathbb C^X$ and $\mathbb C^{X\times X}$ carry the standard orthonormal label and ordered-product bases. If $X\ne\varnothing$, these coordinate spaces are implemented as two ordered registers; if $X=\varnothing$, they are zero spaces and every map below is the unique zero-dimensional map. Define the row-preparation linear map $T:\mathbb C^X\to\mathbb C^{X\times X}$ and the swap $S$ on basis vectors by

$$T|x\rangle=|x\rangle\otimes\sum_{y\in X}\sqrt{P_{xy}}|y\rangle,\qquad S|x,y\rangle=|y,x\rangle.$$

Every scalar square root is the unique nonnegative real root. Define the **discriminant** by $D:=T^*ST$, using the adjoint characterized by $\langle Tv,w\rangle=\langle v,T^*w\rangle$ for the root inner product, which is linear in its first argument. The row-preparation map is an isometry; its complete verification is [[thm-qa-17-discriminant-self-adjoint]]. This is the general row-stochastic construction and assumes no reversibility.

A **finite row-stochastic kernel** is a finite set $X$ and a matrix $P=(P_{xy})_{x,y\in X}$ with $P_{xy}\in[0,1]$ and

$$\sum_{y\in X}P_{xy}=1\qquad(x\in X).$$

The row convention is $P_{xy}=\Pr(Y=y\mid X=x)$: distributions are row vectors and one transition sends $\mu$ to $\mu P$. If $X=\varnothing$, the row conditions are vacuous and there is no probability distribution on $X$. No stationary distribution, reversibility, irreducibility, aperiodicity, or efficient circuit access is part of this definition.
Every linear map $T:V\to W$ between finite-dimensional real or complex inner product spaces has a unique adjoint $T^*:W\to V$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be an endomorphism. The endomorphism $T$ is **self-adjoint** when

$$T^*=T,$$

and **normal** when

$$TT^*=T^*T,$$

where $T^*$ is the adjoint from
[[def-adjoint-of-a-linear-map-between-inner-product-spaces]].

Every self-adjoint endomorphism is normal, because $TT^*=T^2=T^*T$.

If $(e_0,\ldots,e_{r-1})$ is a finite orthonormal list and $v$ is any vector, then

$$\sum_{i<r}|\langle v,e_i\rangle|^2\le\lVert v\rVert^2.$$

Equality holds exactly when $v\in\operatorname{span}(e_0,\ldots,e_{r-1})$. If the list is an orthonormal basis, then for all $v,w$,

$$v=\sum_{i<r}\langle v,e_i\rangle e_i,\qquad \langle v,w\rangle=\sum_{i<r}\langle v,e_i\rangle\overline{\langle w,e_i\rangle},$$

and

$$\lVert v\rVert^2=\sum_{i<r}|\langle v,e_i\rangle|^2.$$

The empty-list case is included.

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

derivations.claim: If $X=\varnothing$, the domain and codomain are zero spaces, so $T^*T=I_0$ and $D$ is the zero endomorphism. Assume now $X\ne\varnothing$. For basis labels $x,x'$, the first register gives $\langle T|x\rangle,T|x'\rangle\rangle=0$ when $x\ne x'$, while for $x=x'$ the value is $\sum_yP_{xy}=1$ by [F2]. Hence the images of the orthonormal basis are orthonormal, which by expansion of arbitrary vectors proves $T$ is an isometry. Moreover, for all $x,x'$, [F3] gives $\langle |x\rangle,T^*T|x'\rangle=\langle T|x\rangle,T|x'\rangle=\langle |x\rangle,|x'\rangle$. Sesquilinearity extends this equality to pairings against every vector; conjugate symmetry and nondegeneracy [F9] then give $T^*T|x'\rangle=|x'\rangle$. Therefore $T^*T=I$.

With the linear-first root inner product, the matrix entry is $D_{xy}=\langle D e_y,e_x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}=\overline{\langle e_x,D e_y\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}}=\overline{\langle T e_x,S T e_y\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}}$ by [F3]. Expanding the two row states, only $|x,y\rangle$ overlaps, with real coefficient $\sqrt{P_{xy}P_{yx}}$; hence $D_{xy}=\sqrt{P_{xy}P_{yx}}$.

For any $w$ in the product space, Parseval in the domain basis and [F3] give $\|T^*w\|^2=\sum_x|\langle T^*w,|x\rangle\rangle|^2=\sum_x|\langle w,T|x\rangle\rangle|^2$. The vectors $T|x\rangle$ are orthonormal by step 1.1, so Bessel's inequality [F5] makes this sum at most $\|w\|^2$.

The formula in step 2.1 is unchanged by exchanging $x,y$ and is real, so $D$ is represented by a real symmetric matrix in the orthonormal label basis. Therefore $D^*=D$ and $D$ is self-adjoint by [F4].

If $X=\varnothing$, then the domain is zero and [F8] gives $\|D\|=0$. Otherwise, for every unit vector $v$, $\|Dv\|=\|T^*STv\|\le\|STv\|=\|Tv\|=1$, using step 2.2, the swap's basis-permutation norm preservation, and step 1.1. Taking the maximum over the nonempty unit sphere proves $\|D\|\le1$; [F8] ensures the finite-dimensional maximum exists.

If $v\ne0$ and $Dv=\lambda v$, self-adjointness gives $\lambda\|v\|^2=\langle Dv,v\rangle=\langle v,Dv\rangle=\overline\lambda\|v\|^2$, so $\lambda$ is real by [F10]. Step 3.2, applied after scaling $v$ to a unit vector, gives $|\lambda|\|v\|=\|Dv\|\le\|v\|$; hence $|\lambda|\le1$.

In the reversible case, detailed balance and $\pi_y>0$ give $P_{yx}=\pi_xP_{xy}/\pi_y$. Since $P_{xy}\ge0$, step 2.1 becomes $D_{xy}=P_{xy}\sqrt{\pi_x/\pi_y}$, exactly the $(x,y)$ entry of $\operatorname{diag}(\sqrt\pi)P\operatorname{diag}(1/\sqrt\pi)$.

For every finite row-stochastic kernel, the map $T$ of [[def-qa-17-szegedy-transition-isometry]] satisfies $T^*T=I$ and is an isometry, and the matrix entries of $D=T^*ST$ are

$$D_{xy}=\sqrt{P_{xy}P_{yx}}.$$

Hence $D$ is real symmetric, self-adjoint, and $\|D\|\le1$. If $(X,P,\pi)$ is also finite reversible, then

$$D=\operatorname{diag}(\sqrt\pi)\,P\,\operatorname{diag}(1/\sqrt\pi).$$

Every eigenvalue of $D$ is real and belongs to $[-1,1]$. The empty state set has the zero endomorphism and empty spectrum; the similarity assertion is only made when a positive stationary probability vector is supplied.

For the finite row-stochastic kernel and row-preparation map of [[def-qa-17-szegedy-transition-isometry]], let $\Pi:=TT^*$, the orthogonal projection onto $\operatorname{ran}(T)$, and choose the reflection sign

$$R_A:=2\Pi-I.$$

With $S$ the two-register swap, define the one-reflection Szegedy step and its square by

$$U:=S R_A,\qquad W:=U^2=(S R_A S)R_A=(2S\Pi S-I)(2\Pi-I).$$

Products act right to left. This fixes $U$ and $W$ as different operators. Algebraically, if $Uv=\mu v$, then $Wv=\mu^2v$ on the same vector. The other common reflection sign is $I-2\Pi=-R_A$ and is not interchangeable inside a controlled operation.

An endomorphism $P$ of a finite-dimensional inner product space is the orthogonal projection onto some subspace if and only if

$$P^2=P\qquad\text{and}\qquad P^*=P.$$

In that case it is the orthogonal projection onto $\operatorname{im}P$, along $\ker P=(\operatorname{im}P)^\perp$. The cases $P=0$ and $P=I$ are included.

A linear map $T:V\to W$ ([[def-linear-map]]) between inner product spaces ([[def-inner-product-space]]) is a **linear isometry** if

$$\lVert Tv\rVert=\lVert v\rVert$$

for every $v\in V$, where the norm is the induced norm [[def-inner-product-norm]]. An invertible linear isometry from a real finite-dimensional inner product space to itself is an **orthogonal operator**; over $\mathbb C$ it is a **unitary operator**.

Equivalently, once the finite-dimensional characterisation is proved, orthogonal and unitary operators are the endomorphisms satisfying $T^*T=TT^*=I$.

Let $V,W$ be inner product spaces ([[def-inner-product-space]]) over the same field and let $T:V\to W$ be linear ([[def-linear-map]]). An **adjoint** of $T$ is a linear map $T^*:W\to V$ such that

By axiom (V1) the triple $(V, +, 0_V)$ is an abelian group ([[def-group]]), hence
in particular a commutative monoid ([[def-semigroup-and-monoid]]). So the finite
products of [[def-monoid-finite-product]] are available in it, and we write them
**additively**: for $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and a finite list $u : n \to V$, that is a
function on the von Neumann natural $n = \{0, \dots, n-1\}$
([[def-natural-numbers]], [[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]),

$$\sum_{i<n} u_i \;:=\; \prod_{i<n} u_i \quad \text{computed in } (V,+,0_V),$$

so that $\sum_{i<0} u_i = 0_V$ and $\sum_{i<\sigma(n)} u_i = \bigl(\sum_{i<n} u_i\bigr) + u_n$,
and the value depends only on $u_0, \dots, u_{n-1}$.

A **linear combination in $V$** is a vector of the form

$$\sum_{i<n} \lambda_i v_i$$

where $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $\lambda : n \to F$ is a finite list of scalars and
$v : n \to V$ is a finite list of vectors; the sum is the finite sum just
described, of the list $i \mapsto \lambda_i v_i$. For $S \subseteq V$, a vector

$n \in \mathbb{N}$, $\lambda : n \to F$ and $v : n \to S$ with

Let $K$ be a probability kernel on a measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$
([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]), and let $\pi$ be a
probability measure on $(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). The
probability measure $\pi$ is **invariant** for $K$, and $\pi$ is a
**stationary distribution** of $K$, when

$$(\pi K)(A):=\int_E K(x,A)\,\pi(dx)=\pi(A)\qquad\text{for every }A\in\mathcal E .$$

The set function $\pi K$ is again a probability measure: for fixed $A$ the map
$x\mapsto K(x,A)$ is measurable and lies in $[0,1]$, so the integral exists in
$[0,1]$; for pairwise disjoint $A_n\in\mathcal E$ the identity
$K(x,\bigcup_nA_n)=\sum_nK(x,A_n)$ of the measure $K(x,\cdot)$ and the
monotone convergence theorem for nonnegative functions
([[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]) give
$\sigma$-additivity of $\pi K$; and $K(x,E)=1$ for every $x$ gives
$(\pi K)(E)=1$. Thus $(\pi K)(A)=\pi(A)$ is an identity between two probability
measures evaluated at $A$.

$\pi K=\pi$. Stationarity of the process is a statement about all of its
finite-dimensional laws and is proved, not assumed, from $\pi K=\pi$; see
[[thm-invariant-initial-law-makes-the-chain-stationary]].

A **finite reversible Markov chain** is a finite row-stochastic kernel $(X,P)$ together with a supplied probability vector $\pi=(\pi_x)_{x\in X}$ such that $\pi_x>0$ for every $x$, $\sum_x\pi_x=1$, $\pi P=\pi$, and

$$\pi_xP_{xy}=\pi_yP_{yx}\qquad(x,y\in X).$$

The stationary law and detailed balance are explicit input hypotheses; the definition does not invoke a theorem that produces a stationary law. No irreducibility or aperiodicity is assumed. In particular, a periodic reversible chain is included.

For $x\in E$, let

$$R_x:=\{n\in\mathbb N:n\ge1\text{ and }p^{(n)}(x,x)>0\}.$$

If $R_x=\varnothing$, set $d(x):=0$. If $R_x\ne\varnothing$, define $d(x)$ to be the greatest positive integer dividing every element of $R_x$ (the gcd convention of [[def-common-divisor-and-gcd]]). This greatest divisor exists: fix one $t\in R_x$; every common positive divisor of $R_x$ is a divisor of $t$, so the set of such divisors is a nonempty finite subset of the positive divisors of $t$, and therefore has a greatest element. The set being maximized is intrinsic to $R_x$, so the result is independent of the auxiliary $t$. Only positive return times enter; $p^{(0)}(x,x)=1$ does not force $d(x)=1$.

For a finite reversible chain $(X,P,\pi)$, let $H_0=\{f:\sum_x\pi_xf_x=0\}$ with the weighted inner product from [[lem-qa-17-reversible-transition-self-adjoint-on-l2-pi]]. Define its **absolute spectral gap** by

$$\delta_{\mathrm{abs}}(P):=1-\|P|_{H_0}\|_{2,\pi}.$$

The norm of the restriction to the zero subspace is $0$ by [[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]], so a one-state chain has absolute gap $1$. No irreducibility or aperiodicity is built into this definition: a reducible chain with a nonconstant stationary vector in $H_0$ can have gap $0$, and a periodic chain can have gap $0$ because of an eigenvalue $-1$. The eigenvalue form of the definition is proved in [[thm-qa-17-absolute-gap-eigenvalue-characterization]].

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ and let $T:V\to V$ be linear. A scalar $\lambda\in F$ is an **eigenvalue** of $T$ when there is a nonzero vector $v\in V$ such that

$$T(v)=\lambda v.$$

Such a vector is an **eigenvector belonging to $\lambda$**. The **eigenspace** belonging to $\lambda$ is

$$E_\lambda(T):=\ker(T-\lambda I_V)=\{v\in V:T(v)=\lambda v\}.$$

Thus $E_\lambda(T)$ is a linear subspace and always contains $0_V$, while $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue exactly when $E_\lambda(T)\ne\{0_V\}$. The **spectrum of $T$ over $F$** is

$$\sigma_F(T):=\{\lambda\in F:\lambda\text{ is an eigenvalue of }T\}.$$

In particular, the unique endomorphism of the zero space has empty spectrum.

derivations.claim: Both rows of $P$ sum to one, $\pi P=\pi$, and $\pi_0P_{01}=\pi_1P_{10}=1/2$; the diagonal detailed-balance equations are automatic. Hence $(X,P,\pi)$ is a finite reversible chain.
Starting from either state, a return occurs exactly at positive even times, so the return-time set is $\{2,4,6,\ldots\}$ and its gcd is $2$. The chain is period two.

The constant vector $\mathbf1=(1,1)$ has eigenvalue $1$, while $h=(1,-1)$ spans $H_0$ and satisfies $Ph=-h$. Thus the restriction to $H_0$ has norm $1$, so [F3] gives $\delta_{\mathrm{abs}}(P)=0$. The eigenvalues of $P$ are exactly $1$ and $-1$.

A **finite reversible Markov chain** is a finite row-stochastic kernel $(X,P)$ together with a supplied probability vector $\pi=(\pi_x)_{x\in X}$ such that $\pi_x>0$ for every $x$, $\sum_x\pi_x=1$, $\pi P=\pi$, and

$$\pi_xP_{xy}=\pi_yP_{yx}\qquad(x,y\in X).$$

The stationary law and detailed balance are explicit input hypotheses; the definition does not invoke a theorem that produces a stationary law. No irreducibility or aperiodicity is assumed. In particular, a periodic reversible chain is included.

For every finite row-stochastic kernel, the map $T$ of [[def-qa-17-szegedy-transition-isometry]] satisfies $T^*T=I$ and is an isometry, and the matrix entries of $D=T^*ST$ are

$$D_{xy}=\sqrt{P_{xy}P_{yx}}.$$

Hence $D$ is real symmetric, self-adjoint, and $\|D\|\le1$. If $(X,P,\pi)$ is also finite reversible, then

$$D=\operatorname{diag}(\sqrt\pi)\,P\,\operatorname{diag}(1/\sqrt\pi).$$

Every eigenvalue of $D$ is real and belongs to $[-1,1]$. The empty state set has the zero endomorphism and empty spectrum; the similarity assertion is only made when a positive stationary probability vector is supplied.

For a finite row-stochastic kernel $(X,P)$, let $\mathbb C^X$ and $\mathbb C^{X\times X}$ carry the standard orthonormal label and ordered-product bases. If $X\ne\varnothing$, these coordinate spaces are implemented as two ordered registers; if $X=\varnothing$, they are zero spaces and every map below is the unique zero-dimensional map. Define the row-preparation linear map $T:\mathbb C^X\to\mathbb C^{X\times X}$ and the swap $S$ on basis vectors by

$$T|x\rangle=|x\rangle\otimes\sum_{y\in X}\sqrt{P_{xy}}|y\rangle,\qquad S|x,y\rangle=|y,x\rangle.$$

Every scalar square root is the unique nonnegative real root. Define the **discriminant** by $D:=T^*ST$, using the adjoint characterized by $\langle Tv,w\rangle=\langle v,T^*w\rangle$ for the root inner product, which is linear in its first argument. The row-preparation map is an isometry; its complete verification is [[thm-qa-17-discriminant-self-adjoint]]. This is the general row-stochastic construction and assumes no reversibility.

For the finite row-stochastic kernel and row-preparation map of [[def-qa-17-szegedy-transition-isometry]], let $\Pi:=TT^*$, the orthogonal projection onto $\operatorname{ran}(T)$, and choose the reflection sign

$$R_A:=2\Pi-I.$$

With $S$ the two-register swap, define the one-reflection Szegedy step and its square by

$$U:=S R_A,\qquad W:=U^2=(S R_A S)R_A=(2S\Pi S-I)(2\Pi-I).$$

Products act right to left. This fixes $U$ and $W$ as different operators. Algebraically, if $Uv=\mu v$, then $Wv=\mu^2v$ on the same vector. The other common reflection sign is $I-2\Pi=-R_A$ and is not interchangeable inside a controlled operation.

For any eigenpair $Dv=\lambda v$ with $v\ne0$ and $\lambda\in[-1,1]$, put $a:=Tv$ and $b:=STv$. Then $\operatorname{span}\{a,b\}$ is invariant under $U$, and

$$U a=b,\qquad U b=-a+2\lambda b.$$

All eigenvalues of $D$ satisfy the displayed interval hypothesis by [[thm-qa-17-discriminant-self-adjoint]]. If $\lambda=1$ or $\lambda=-1$, then $b=\lambda a$ and the span is one-dimensional. If $-1<\lambda<1$, the two vectors are linearly independent and the invariant subspace is two-dimensional.

For the projection $\Pi=TT^*$ onto $A=\operatorname{ran}(T)$, the operators $R_A=2\Pi-I$ and $S$ are self-adjoint involutions. Hence $U=SR_A$ and $W=U^2$ are unitary. On $A^\perp$, $\Pi=0$ and therefore $U=-S$.

Let $D=T^*ST$ be the discriminant of a finite row-stochastic kernel and let $U=S(2TT^*-I)$ and $W=U^2$. For every eigenvalue $\lambda\in(-1,1)$ of $D$, counted with multiplicity, its invariant planes contribute eigenvalues

$$\exp(i\arccos\lambda),\ \exp(-i\arccos\lambda)\quad\text{for }U,\qquad \exp(2i\arccos\lambda),\ \exp(-2i\arccos\lambda)\quad\text{for }W.$$

For each eigendirection with $\lambda=1$ (respectively $\lambda=-1$), the plane collapses to a line on which $U$ acts as $+I$ (respectively $-I$), so $W$ acts as $+I$. On the remaining subspace $K=(\operatorname{ran}T+\operatorname{ran}(ST))^\perp$, $U=-S$ and its eigenvalues lie in $\{+1,-1\}$; therefore all eigenvalues of $W$ there are $+1$. If $X=\varnothing$, both spaces are zero and the statements about eigenvalues are vacuous.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ and let $T:V\to V$ be linear. A scalar $\lambda\in F$ is an **eigenvalue** of $T$ when there is a nonzero vector $v\in V$ such that

$$T(v)=\lambda v.$$

Such a vector is an **eigenvector belonging to $\lambda$**. The **eigenspace** belonging to $\lambda$ is

$$E_\lambda(T):=\ker(T-\lambda I_V)=\{v\in V:T(v)=\lambda v\}.$$

Thus $E_\lambda(T)$ is a linear subspace and always contains $0_V$, while $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue exactly when $E_\lambda(T)\ne\{0_V\}$. The **spectrum of $T$ over $F$** is

$$\sigma_F(T):=\{\lambda\in F:\lambda\text{ is an eigenvalue of }T\}.$$

In particular, the unique endomorphism of the zero space has empty spectrum.

For a linear map $T:V\to W$, its **kernel** and **image** are respectively

$$\ker T:=\{v\in V:T(v)=0_W\},\qquad \operatorname{im}T:=\{T(v):v\in V\}.$$

That both sets are linear subspaces, and that a trivial kernel characterises
injectivity, is proved in [[thm-linear-kernel-image-and-injectivity]].

For a linear map $T:V\to W$, the sets $\ker T$ and $\operatorname{im}T$ are
linear subspaces. Moreover, $T$ is injective if and only if $\ker T=\{0_V\}$.

For a linear subspace $W$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]) of an inner product space $V$, using the preceding notion of orthogonality ([[def-orthogonal-vectors-sets-and-orthonormal-bases]]), its **orthogonal complement** is

$$W^\perp:=\{v\in V:\langle v,w\rangle=0\text{ for every }w\in W\}.$$

This is a linear subspace: $0\in W^\perp$, and linearity in the first argument shows that $au+bv\in W^\perp$ whenever $u,v\in W^\perp$ and $a,b$ are scalars. One has $V^\perp=\{0\}$ by positive definiteness and $\{0\}^\perp=V$.

If $W$ is a subspace of a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space $V$, then

$$V=W\oplus W^\perp.$$

Thus every $v\in V$ has unique vectors $w\in W$ and $z\in W^\perp$ with $v=w+z$.

derivations.claim: Both rows of $P_a$ sum to one, $\pi P_a=\pi$, and $P_a$ is symmetric, so $\pi_x(P_a)_{xy}=\pi_y(P_a)_{yx}$ for all $x,y$. Thus $\pi$ is a positive stationary reversible law.
Since $P_a$ is symmetric and has nonnegative entries, [F2] gives $D=P_a$. The vectors $u_+=(1,1)$ and $u_-=(1,-1)$ form a basis with $Du_+=u_+$ and $Du_-=(1-2a)u_-$.

At $a=0$, $T|0\rangle=|00\rangle$ and $T|1\rangle=|11\rangle$, so $A=B=\operatorname{span}\{|00\rangle,|11\rangle\}$. On $A$, $R_A=2TT^*-I$ is $+I$ and $S=I$, so $U=+I$. On $K=\operatorname{span}\{|01\rangle,|10\rangle\}$, [F6] gives $U=-S$, whose eigenvectors $|01\rangle+|10\rangle$ and $|01\rangle-|10\rangle$ have eigenvalues $-1$ and $+1$. Hence $\sigma_{\mathrm{mult}}(U)=\{1,1,1,-1\}$ and $W=I$ has four eigenvalues $+1$.

At $a=1$, $T|0\rangle=|01\rangle$ and $T|1\rangle=|10\rangle$, so $A=B=\operatorname{span}\{|01\rangle,|10\rangle\}$. On $A$, $R_A=+I$ and $U=S$, with eigenvalues $+1,-1$. On $K=\operatorname{span}\{|00\rangle,|11\rangle\}$, $S=I$, so [F6] gives $U=-I$. Thus $\sigma_{\mathrm{mult}}(U)=\{1,-1,-1,-1\}$ and $W=I$ has four eigenvalues $+1$.

Suppose $0<a<1$ and set $\lambda=1-2a\in(-1,1)$ and $\theta=\arccos\lambda\in(0,\pi)$. By [F7], the $u_+$ endpoint line contributes $+1$ to $U$ and $W$, and the $u_-$ invariant plane contributes $e^{i\theta},e^{-i\theta}$ to $U$ and $e^{2i\theta},e^{-2i\theta}$ to $W$.

Under the hypothesis of step 2.1, put $r=\sqrt{1-a}$ and $s=\sqrt a$. Let $A=\operatorname{im}T$ and $B=\operatorname{im}(ST)$; these are subspaces by [F9]–[F10]. By [F3], their spanning vectors are $T|0\rangle=r|00\rangle+s|01\rangle$, $T|1\rangle=s|10\rangle+r|11\rangle$, $ST|0\rangle=r|00\rangle+s|10\rangle$, and $ST|1\rangle=s|01\rangle+r|11\rangle$. The vector $k=(s|00\rangle-r|01\rangle-r|10\rangle+s|11\rangle)/\sqrt2$ has norm one because $r^2+s^2=1$ and is orthogonal to each spanning vector by cancellation of the two $rs$ terms. Hence [F11] gives $0\ne k\in K:=(A+B)^\perp$; since the product register has dimension four, [F12] implies $\dim(A+B)\le3$. By [F5], $STu_+=Tu_+$ gives a common nonzero vector in $A\cap B$, while $Tu_-$ and $STu_-$ are linearly independent because $-1<\lambda<1$. These two vectors are orthogonal to the common vector: $\langle Tu_+,Tu_-\rangle=\langle STu_+,STu_-\rangle=0$ by isometry of $T$ and unitarity of $S$, and $\langle Tu_+,STu_-\rangle=\langle u_+,Du_-\rangle=0$ by the distinct eigenvalues in step 1.2; the reverse cross-pairing vanishes by conjugate symmetry. Thus $\dim(A+B)\ge3$, so it is exactly $3$ and $K$ is one-dimensional, hence $K=\operatorname{span}\{k\}$. The coefficients of $|01\rangle$ and $|10\rangle$ in $k$ are equal, so [F3] gives $Sk=k$. By [F6], $U=-S=-I$ on $K$. Combining this complement eigenvalue with the line and plane eigenvalues from step 2.1 yields $\sigma_{\mathrm{mult}}(U)=\{1,-1,e^{i\theta},e^{-i\theta}\}$ and $\sigma_{\mathrm{mult}}(W)=\{1,1,e^{2i\theta},e^{-2i\theta}\}$.
